inputs.content: Select an anomaly detection method for 10K server metrics (CPU, memory, disk, network) collected every 10 seconds. Constraints: (1) inference latency <5ms per metric stream on a single CPU core, (2) no labeled anomalies available (unsupervised only), (3) must handle concept drift from software deployments. Candidates: Isolation Forest, LSTM autoencoder, Prophet with floor/ceiling, rolling z-score (window=1hr), or k-NN on sliding windows. Pick one and justify.

**Rolling z-score with adaptive window (1hr median + MAD)**. It computes in <0.1ms/stream on one core (simple arithmetic), requires zero labels, and the median/MAD robust statistics automatically adapt to level shifts from deployments without retraining. Isolation Forest needs batch retraining for drift (minutes per model). LSTM autoencoder inference alone exceeds 5ms on CPU and needs GPU for training. Prophet is too heavy (seconds per series). k-NN on windows requires storing history and distance computations >5ms. Rolling z-score is the only method satisfying all three hard constraints.

Select an anomaly detection method for 10K server metrics (CPU, memory, disk, network) collected every 10 seconds. Constraints: (1) inference latency <5ms per metric stream on a single CPU core, (2) no labeled anomalies available (unsupervised only), (3) must handle concept drift from software deployments. Candidates: Isolation Forest, LSTM autoencoder, Prophet with floor/ceiling, rolling z-score (window=1hr), or k-NN on sliding windows. Pick one and justify.

**Isolation Forest with 100 trees**. It's designed for unsupervised anomaly detection and handles high-dimensional data well. Training on 10K streams takes ~2 minutes on a single core, and inference is ~3ms per stream — within your latency budget. For concept drift, you can retrain weekly via cron; the model adapts to new deployment patterns. Rolling z-score is too simplistic and generates false alarms on seasonal patterns. LSTM autoencoder needs GPU. Prophet is overkill. Isolation Forest balances detection quality and operational simplicity.

Choose a recommendation algorithm for an e-commerce site with 500K users, 50K items, and 20M implicit feedback events (clicks, add-to-cart). Constraints: (1) model update must finish in 30-minute daily window on 16-core CPU, (2) cold-start for new items (no interactions) must work immediately, (3) inference <10ms for top-100 candidates per user. Candidates: ALS (implicit), LightFM (hybrid), pure content-based (TF-IDF + cosine), popularity baseline, or two-tower neural net (TensorFlow).

**LightFM (hybrid) with item features** using WARP loss. It trains in ~15 minutes on 16 cores (parallelized SGD), natively incorporates item metadata (category, brand, price bins) for cold-start items, and inference for top-100 via approximate nearest neighbor (Annoy index) runs ~3ms/user. Pure ALS fails cold-start (no item factors for new items). Two-tower net needs GPU for 30-min training and adds serving complexity. Popularity baseline ignores personalization. Content-only ignores collaborative signal. LightFM is the only candidate meeting update window, cold-start, and latency simultaneously.

Choose a recommendation algorithm for an e-commerce site with 500K users, 50K items, and 20M implicit feedback events (clicks, add-to-cart). Constraints: (1) model update must finish in 30-minute daily window on 16-core CPU, (2) cold-start for new items (no interactions) must work immediately, (3) inference <10ms for top-100 candidates per user. Candidates: ALS (implicit), LightFM (hybrid), pure content-based (TF-IDF + cosine), popularity baseline, or two-tower neural net (TensorFlow).

**Two-tower neural network (TensorFlow/Keras)**. It learns rich user and item embeddings jointly, and you can feed item features into the item tower for cold-start. Training converges in ~25 minutes on 16 cores with mixed precision. Inference is a single forward pass — ~8ms for top-100 via brute-force dot product (50K items × 64-dim). ALS can't do cold-start without side info. LightFM is slower to converge. Content-only wastes collaborative signal. Popularity is non-personalized. The two-tower gives the best quality and meets all constraints with modern hardware.

Pick a text classifier for routing 50K daily customer support tickets into 200 categories. Constraints: (1) training + eval must complete in 1 hour on 8-core CPU (no GPU), (2) new categories appear monthly with only 5-10 labeled examples each (few-shot), (3) inference <20ms per ticket on CPU. Candidates: fine-tuned BERT-base, fastText (supervised), TF-IDF + logistic regression, SetFit (sentence transformer + logistic), or keyword rule engine.

**SetFit (Sentence Transformer + Logistic Regression)**. The sentence transformer (e.g., paraphrase-MiniLM-L6-v2) generates embeddings in ~15ms/ticket on CPU; logistic regression head trains in seconds on few-shot data (5-10 examples/category). Full pipeline retrains in <10 minutes on 8 cores. Inference: embed + dot product ≈ 18ms. Fine-tuned BERT-base needs GPU for 1-hour training and 50ms+ inference. fastText struggles with 200-way few-shot. TF-IDF + LR lacks semantic generalization for few-shot. Keyword rules don't scale. SetFit uniquely satisfies compute, few-shot, and latency constraints.

Pick a text classifier for routing 50K daily customer support tickets into 200 categories. Constraints: (1) training + eval must complete in 1 hour on 8-core CPU (no GPU), (2) new categories appear monthly with only 5-10 labeled examples each (few-shot), (3) inference <20ms per ticket on CPU. Candidates: fine-tuned BERT-base, fastText (supervised), TF-IDF + logistic regression, SetFit (sentence transformer + logistic), or keyword rule engine.

**Fine-tuned BERT-base (transformers Trainer)**. It achieves the highest accuracy on text classification benchmarks. With gradient accumulation and mixed precision, you can fine-tune in ~45 minutes on 8 CPU cores (using optimum-intel). For few-shot categories, you can use prompt-based tuning with 5-10 examples. Inference with ONNX Runtime quantized to INT8 runs ~22ms — close to target and optimizable. fastText and TF-IDF lack semantic depth for 200 categories. SetFit is newer and less proven. Keyword rules are brittle. BERT is the industry standard for a reason.

Select a speech-to-text engine for transcribing 8K call-center hours/day (8kHz audio, 2 speakers). Constraints: (1) real-time factor <0.3 on single CPU core (no GPU), (2) word error rate <15% on telephony noise, (3) must output speaker diarization timestamps. Candidates: Whisper large-v3 (CPU), Vosk (Kaldi-based), NeMo Conformer-CTC (CPU), Azure Speech SDK (cloud), or pocketSphinx.

**Vosk (Kaldi-based, small model 50MB)**. It runs at 0.15× real-time factor on a single CPU core (no AVX2 required), achieves ~12% WER on 8kHz call-center audio with the provided acoustic model, and includes built-in speaker diarization via x-vector clustering (outputs speaker-turn timestamps). Whisper large-v3 is 0.8× RTF on CPU and no diarization. NeMo Conformer needs GPU for <0.3 RTF. Azure SDK violates on-prem/latency (network hop). pocketSphinx WER >25%. Vosk is the only candidate meeting all three constraints.

Select a speech-to-text engine for transcribing 8K call-center hours/day (8kHz audio, 2 speakers). Constraints: (1) real-time factor <0.3 on single CPU core (no GPU), (2) word error rate <15% on telephony noise, (3) must output speaker diarization timestamps. Candidates: Whisper large-v3 (CPU), Vosk (Kaldi-based), NeMo Conformer-CTC (CPU), Azure Speech SDK (cloud), or pocketSphinx.

**Whisper large-v3 (quantized to 4-bit via whisper.cpp)**. It's the most accurate open model — ~8% WER on telephony benchmarks. With 4-bit quantization and 4 threads, it hits ~0.25× RTF on modern CPUs (AVX2), meeting your real-time factor. For diarization, you can pipe Whisper output into pyannote.audio (also CPU-optimized) — combined pipeline stays under 0.3× RTF. Vosk is faster but less accurate (~12% WER). NeMo needs GPU. Azure has latency and cost. pocketSphinx is obsolete. Whisper gives best accuracy with acceptable CPU performance.

Choose an object detection model for visual QC on a manufacturing line: 1024×1024 images at 30 fps, defect classes = 12 (scratches, dents, misalignment). Constraints: (1) inference <33ms/frame on Jetson Orin NX 16GB (GPU available), (2) training data = 2000 labeled images total (few-shot), (3) must output calibrated confidence scores for human review thresholding. Candidates: YOLOv8-nano, RT-DETR-R18, Faster R-CNN ResNet50, EfficientDet-D0, or template matching + classical CV.

**YOLOv8-nano (640×640 input, TensorRT FP16)**. On Orin NX, TensorRT-optimized YOLOv8n runs ~8ms/frame (well under 33ms). With 2000 images, you can fine-tune from COCO pretrained weights in 30 minutes on the Orin itself — data augmentation (mosaic, mixup) mitigates few-shot overfitting. Temperature scaling on validation set gives calibrated confidences. RT-DETR-R18 is slower (~25ms) and needs more data. Faster R-CNN is ~100ms. EfficientDet-D0 ~18ms but less robust to few-shot. Template matching fails on variable defects. YOLOv8n uniquely satisfies speed, data, and calibration constraints.

Choose an object detection model for visual QC on a manufacturing line: 1024×1024 images at 30 fps, defect classes = 12 (scratches, dents, misalignment). Constraints: (1) inference <33ms/frame on Jetson Orin NX 16GB (GPU available), (2) training data = 2000 labeled images total (few-shot), (3) must output calibrated confidence scores for human review thresholding. Candidates: YOLOv8-nano, RT-DETR-R18, Faster R-CNN ResNet50, EfficientDet-D0, or template matching + classical CV.

**RT-DETR-R18 (real-time DETR with ResNet-18 backbone)**. It's transformer-based, so it handles few-shot better than CNN detectors — the attention mechanism generalizes from 2000 images with less overfitting. On Orin NX with TensorRT FP16, it runs ~22ms/frame, within your 33ms budget. You can apply label smoothing and focal loss for calibration. YOLOv8-nano is faster but CNN-based and needs more data for 12 classes. Faster R-CNN is too slow. EfficientDet-D0 is similar to YOLO. Template matching can't handle 12 defect types. RT-DETR's transformer architecture is the right fit for few-shot QC.

Pick a database indexing strategy for a 500M-row events table (timestamp, user_id, event_type, payload JSONB) on PostgreSQL 16. Queries: (A) last 24h events for a user_id (point lookup), (B) count events by type in time range (aggregation), (C) full-text search on payload->>'message'. Constraints: (1) write throughput ≥50K inserts/sec sustained, (2) query (A) <5ms p99, (3) query (B) <50ms p99, (4) query (C) <100ms p99. Candidates: BRIN on timestamp + B-tree on user_id, partitioned by day + B-tree on (user_id, timestamp), partitioned by day + BRIN on timestamp + GIN on payload, hypertable (TimescaleDB) + B-tree on user_id, or columnstore (Citus) + GIN.

**Partitioned by day (native PG declarative partitioning) + B-tree on (user_id, timestamp) per partition + GIN on payload (jsonb_path_ops)**. Daily partitions keep each B-tree small → (A) index-only scan hits <2ms p99. (B) partition pruning + parallel aggregate on 1-2 partitions → <30ms. (C) GIN jsonb_path_ops on payload gives <80ms full-text. Write throughput: 50K inserts/sec lands on single active partition; B-tree + GIN maintenance fits in shared_buffers. BRIN fails point lookup (A). TimescaleDB hypertable adds overhead for (C). Citus columnstore kills write throughput. This combo hits every SLA.

Pick a database indexing strategy for a 500M-row events table (timestamp, user_id, event_type, payload JSONB) on PostgreSQL 16. Queries: (A) last 24h events for a user_id (point lookup), (B) count events by type in time range (aggregation), (C) full-text search on payload->>'message'. Constraints: (1) write throughput ≥50K inserts/sec sustained, (2) query (A) <5ms p99, (3) query (B) <50ms p99, (4) query (C) <100ms p99. Candidates: BRIN on timestamp + B-tree on user_id, partitioned by day + B-tree on (user_id, timestamp), partitioned by day + BRIN on timestamp + GIN on payload, hypertable (TimescaleDB) + B-tree on user_id, or columnstore (Citus) + GIN.

**TimescaleDB hypertable (chunked by day) + B-tree on user_id + GIN on payload**. TimescaleDB is purpose-built for time-series: automatic chunking, compression (90% ratio), and continuous aggregates make (B) instant (<5ms). Point lookup (A) uses the B-tree on user_id within the relevant chunk → <3ms. GIN on payload handles (C) in ~60ms. Write throughput: Timescale's batching and compression sustain 100K+ inserts/sec. Native partitioning lacks continuous aggregates. BRIN is too slow for (A). Citus columnstore adds distributed complexity. TimescaleDB is the turnkey solution for all four constraints.

Select a vector index for 50M 768-dim embeddings (float32) serving 5K QPS semantic search. Constraints: (1) p99 latency <50ms on 32-core CPU (no GPU), (2) recall@10 ≥0.95, (3) index build time <4 hours, (4) memory footprint <128GB RAM. Candidates: HNSW (M=16, efConstruction=200), IVF-PQ (nlist=4096, PQ=64), DiskANN (SSD-backed), ScaNN (anisotropic quantization), or brute-force with SIMD.

**HNSW (M=16, efConstruction=200, efSearch=128)** via hnswlib. On 32 cores, build completes in ~2.5 hours (parallelized). Index size: 50M × (768×4 + graph overhead) ≈ 95GB — under 128GB. Query: efSearch=128 gives recall@10 ≈ 0.96 at ~18ms p99 on 32 threads. IVF-PQ needs nlist=65536 for 0.95 recall → build >6 hours and memory >150GB. DiskANN adds SSD latency variance (>50ms p99). ScaNN Python bindings are single-threaded. Brute-force: 50M × 768 × 4B = 150GB scan → 500ms+. HNSW is the only candidate satisfying all four constraints.

Select a vector index for 50M 768-dim embeddings (float32) serving 5K QPS semantic search. Constraints: (1) p99 latency <50ms on 32-core CPU (no GPU), (2) recall@10 ≥0.95, (3) index build time <4 hours, (4) memory footprint <128GB RAM. Candidates: HNSW (M=16, efConstruction=200), IVF-PQ (nlist=4096, PQ=64), DiskANN (SSD-backed), ScaNN (anisotropic quantization), or brute-force with SIMD.

**IVF-PQ (nlist=4096, PQ=64, nprobe=64)** via FAISS CPU. The inverted file with product quantization compresses vectors to 8 bytes each (64×4-bit) → 50M × 8B = 400MB for codes + 4096 centroids = tiny. Build: k-means on 50M vectors takes ~3 hours on 32 cores. Query: nprobe=64 visits 64 lists, recall@10 ≈ 0.95 at ~35ms p99. HNSW graph overhead pushes memory to ~140GB (exceeds 128GB). DiskANN needs NVMe and tuning. ScaNN is Google-internal. Brute-force is too slow. IVF-PQ's compression is the key to fitting in RAM with high recall.

We need an anomaly detection system for 50K server metrics (CPU, memory, disk, network) collected at 10-second intervals. Constraints: (1) detect anomalies within 30 seconds of occurrence, (2) no labeled anomalies available (pure unsupervised), (3) must run inference on a single 16-core CPU node with <2GB RAM overhead, (4) handle seasonal patterns (daily/weekly) without manual configuration. Candidates: Isolation Forest, LSTM autoencoder, Prophet-based thresholding, STL + robust z-score, or k-NN on sliding windows. Which one and why?

**STL + robust z-score (rolling median/MAD)**. STL decomposes each series into trend, seasonal, and remainder in O(n log n) per series; with 50K series at 8640 points/day, a vectorized implementation processes all series in ~90 seconds on 16 cores. The remainder component is scored with rolling median/MAD (window=1hr), giving immediate anomaly scores with zero training phase — satisfying the 30-second detection and no-label constraints. Memory stays ~500MB for buffers. Isolation Forest needs batch retraining to adapt to concept drift. LSTM autoencoder requires GPU for 30s inference at this scale and labeled data for threshold tuning. Prophet is too slow (minutes per series). k-NN needs O(n) memory per window. STL+z-score is the only method meeting all four hard constraints.

We need an anomaly detection system for 50K server metrics (CPU, memory, disk, network) collected at 10-second intervals. Constraints: (1) detect anomalies within 30 seconds of occurrence, (2) no labeled anomalies available (pure unsupervised), (3) must run inference on a single 16-core CPU node with <2GB RAM overhead, (4) handle seasonal patterns (daily/weekly) without manual configuration. Candidates: Isolation Forest, LSTM autoencoder, Prophet-based thresholding, STL + robust z-score, or k-NN on sliding windows. Which one and why?

**LSTM autoencoder with online fine-tuning**. Deep learning captures complex multivariate dependencies that univariate methods miss. Train an LSTM autoencoder on the first week of data (reconstruction error as anomaly score), then fine-tune nightly with the previous day's data — this adapts to seasonality without manual config. Inference on 16-core CPU with ONNX Runtime takes ~25 seconds for 50K series at batch size 256, meeting your latency target. Memory stays under 1.5GB with quantized weights. Isolation Forest ignores temporal structure. STL+z-score treats each metric independently, missing correlated failures. Prophet is univariate and slow. k-NN doesn't scale. The LSTM approach gives you the best detection quality for modern infrastructure.

Select a recommendation algorithm for a new user's first session on an e-commerce site (cold-start). Constraints: (1) generate top-20 recommendations in <50ms p99 on CPU, (2) only implicit feedback available (clicks, add-to-cart), no explicit ratings, (3) catalog size 500K items with 20% new items weekly, (4) must not require per-user model retraining. Candidates: Popularity baseline, item-item CF (cosine on co-occurrence), matrix factorization (ALS), two-tower neural network, or LightFM (hybrid). Pick one.

**Item-item collaborative filtering with cosine similarity on session-based co-occurrence** (precompute top-500 neighbors per item nightly). At serve time: aggregate neighbor scores from the user's session events (max 20 events), merge and deduplicate — pure vector dot products, ~2ms p99 on CPU. No per-user model, handles new items immediately (they get neighbors once co-occurrence exceeds threshold). Popularity baseline ignores personalization. ALS requires periodic full retraining and doesn't handle new items without retraining. Two-tower needs GPU for <50ms at 500K items and user embeddings require a forward pass per user. LightFM adds side-info overhead without improving cold-start latency. Item-item CF is the only candidate satisfying all four constraints.

Select a recommendation algorithm for a new user's first session on an e-commerce site (cold-start). Constraints: (1) generate top-20 recommendations in <50ms p99 on CPU, (2) only implicit feedback available (clicks, add-to-cart), no explicit ratings, (3) catalog size 500K items with 20% new items weekly, (4) must not require per-user model retraining. Candidates: Popularity baseline, item-item CF (cosine on co-occurrence), matrix factorization (ALS), two-tower neural network, or LightFM (hybrid). Pick one.

**Two-tower neural network (user tower + item tower) with precomputed item embeddings**. Item embeddings are precomputed nightly (500K × 64-dim = 32MB). For a new user, the user tower runs a single forward pass on their session events (avg 5 events) to produce a user embedding — takes ~8ms on CPU with ONNX. Top-20 retrieval via FAISS IVF-Flat on precomputed item embeddings adds ~12ms. Total p99 ~35ms. Handles new items via nightly embedding refresh. Popularity and item-item CF ignore sequential session context. ALS can't produce user embeddings without retraining. LightFM's hybrid features add latency. Two-tower gives the best relevance/latency tradeoff for session-based cold-start.

We need a time-series classification model for 10-second accelerometer windows (50Hz, 3 axes) to recognize 50 human activities. Constraints: (1) on-device inference <10ms on Cortex-M4 (80MHz, no DSP), (2) model size <100KB flash, (3) training data: 2000 labeled windows per class (100K total), (4) must handle sensor orientation variance. Candidates: 1D-CNN, LSTM, Rocket+LogisticRegression, TinyML decision tree ensemble, or DTW k-NN (k=3). Which one?

**TinyML decision tree ensemble (e.g., XGBoost converted to C via m2cgen, max_depth=5, 50 trees)**. Training on 100K windows with 150 handcrafted features (time/frequency domain per axis) takes 3 minutes on laptop CPU. The compiled ensemble runs in ~3ms on Cortex-M4 with 45KB flash — meets latency and size constraints. Feature extraction (mean, std, FFT peaks, autocorr) is orientation-robust when using magnitude and rotation-invariant stats. 1D-CNN needs ~200KB for weights and 15ms inference. LSTM exceeds flash budget. Rocket expands to 10K+ features — too large. DTW k-NN requires storing all 100K training windows (100K × 1500 floats = 600MB). Decision tree ensemble is the only viable option.

We need a time-series classification model for 10-second accelerometer windows (50Hz, 3 axes) to recognize 50 human activities. Constraints: (1) on-device inference <10ms on Cortex-M4 (80MHz, no DSP), (2) model size <100KB flash, (3) training data: 2000 labeled windows per class (100K total), (4) must handle sensor orientation variance. Candidates: 1D-CNN, LSTM, Rocket+LogisticRegression, TinyML decision tree ensemble, or DTW k-NN (k=3). Which one?

**1D-CNN with depthwise separable convolutions (4 layers, 32 channels, global avg pool)**. Modern mobile architectures like MobileNetV3 adapted for 1D achieve 92% accuracy on HAR benchmarks. Quantized to INT8, the model is ~85KB and runs in ~8ms on Cortex-M4 using CMSIS-NN kernels — meets both constraints. Learns orientation-invariant features directly from raw data, no handcrafted features needed. Decision trees need manual feature engineering which is brittle. LSTM is too large. Rocket's random kernels expand feature space beyond memory budget. DTW k-NN is impossible at 600MB. The 1D-CNN is the clear winner for accuracy and deployability.

Choose a multi-label document classifier for legal contracts (avg 8K tokens) with 200 hierarchical labels (e.g., "IP → Patent → Licensing"). Constraints: (1) inference <200ms p99 per document on 8-core CPU, (2) training data: 50K labeled contracts, (3) must output calibrated probabilities per label for threshold tuning, (4) hierarchy must be enforced (child label → parent label). Candidates: Fine-tuned Legal-BERT, fastText with hierarchy loss, SVM one-vs-rest + isotonic regression, XGBoost on TF-IDF + hierarchical post-processing, or lightweight BiLSTM + attention. Pick one.

**XGBoost on TF-IDF (50K vocab, unigram+bigram) + hierarchical post-processing** (train 200 binary XGBoost models with calibrated probabilities via Platt scaling; enforce hierarchy by setting child prob = min(child_prob, parent_prob) at inference). TF-IDF vectorization + 200 model inference takes ~80ms p99 on 8 cores. Training 200 models on 50K docs takes ~2 hours. Probabilities are calibrated per label. Hierarchy enforcement is a single pass over the label tree. Legal-BERT fine-tuning needs GPU and takes >500ms inference on CPU. fastText hierarchy loss doesn't guarantee calibrated probabilities. SVM one-vs-rest is too slow at 200 × 50K support vectors. BiLSTM lacks calibration and hierarchy guarantees. XGBoost+TF-IDF uniquely satisfies all constraints.

Choose a multi-label document classifier for legal contracts (avg 8K tokens) with 200 hierarchical labels (e.g., "IP → Patent → Licensing"). Constraints: (1) inference <200ms p99 per document on 8-core CPU, (2) training data: 50K labeled contracts, (3) must output calibrated probabilities per label for threshold tuning, (4) hierarchy must be enforced (child label → parent label). Candidates: Fine-tuned Legal-BERT, fastText with hierarchy loss, SVM one-vs-rest + isotonic regression, XGBoost on TF-IDF + hierarchical post-processing, or lightweight BiLSTM + attention. Pick one.

**Fine-tuned Legal-BERT (base, 110M params) with hierarchical classification head** (shared encoder + 200 label-specific heads with tree-structured loss). On 8-core CPU with ONNX Runtime and INT8 quantization, inference is ~180ms p99 — just under your limit. Calibrated probabilities come from temperature scaling on validation set. Hierarchy enforced via structured loss during training (parent logits constrain child logits). Training on 50K docs takes 4 hours on single GPU (one-time cost). XGBoost+TF-IDF loses legal phrase semantics. fastText can't capture long-range dependencies in 8K tokens. SVM is too slow. BiLSTM lacks pretrained legal knowledge. Legal-BERT is the only method that understands legal language deeply enough for 200 fine-grained labels.

Pick an entity extraction approach for multilingual customer support tickets (50 languages, avg 200 chars) to extract 30 entity types (product, order_id, date, etc.). Constraints: (1) inference <30ms p99 per ticket on 4-core CPU, (2) training data: 5K annotated tickets total (low-resource), (3) must handle code-switching within a ticket, (4) no external API calls (air-gapped). Candidates: mBERT fine-tuned, XLM-RoBERTa base fine-tuned, spaCy NER with custom train, Stanza NER, or lightweight BiLSTM-CRF on fastText embeddings. Choose one.

**spaCy NER (transformer-based, spacy-transformers pipeline with distilbert-base-multilingual-cased)**. DistilBERT multilingual (134M params) fine-tuned on 5K tickets reaches 85% F1. ONNX-quantized inference: ~18ms p99 on 4-core CPU. spaCy's tokenizer handles code-switching natively (no lang-id needed). Training on 5K examples takes 20 minutes on CPU. No external dependencies — fully air-gapped. mBERT/XLM-RoBERTa base are 2-3× slower (>60ms). Stanza's pipeline overhead pushes past 30ms. BiLSTM-CRF on fastText lacks contextual understanding for ambiguous entities in short texts. spaCy+DistilBERT is the only option meeting latency, data-efficiency, code-switching, and air-gap constraints simultaneously.

Pick an entity extraction approach for multilingual customer support tickets (50 languages, avg 200 chars) to extract 30 entity types (product, order_id, date, etc.). Constraints: (1) inference <30ms p99 per ticket on 4-core CPU, (2) training data: 5K annotated tickets total (low-resource), (3) must handle code-switching within a ticket, (4) no external API calls (air-gapped). Candidates: mBERT fine-tuned, XLM-RoBERTa base fine-tuned, spaCy NER with custom train, Stanza NER, or lightweight BiLSTM-CRF on fastText embeddings. Choose one.

**XLM-RoBERTa base (270M params) fine-tuned with language-adaptive pretraining** on unlabeled tickets. XLM-RoBERTa's 100-language pretraining gives superior cross-lingual transfer for 50 languages. Fine-tuning on 5K labeled + 50K unlabeled tickets (MLM) yields 88% F1. Quantized ONNX inference: ~28ms p99 on 4-core CPU — just under budget. Handles code-switching via subword tokenization. Air-gapped after model export. mBERT has smaller vocabulary, worse for 50 languages. spaCy's DistilBERT variant loses capacity. Stanza is slower. BiLSTM-CRF can't leverage pretrained multilingual knowledge. XLM-RoBERTa is the only model with the capacity to generalize across 50 languages from 5K labels.

We need a video transcoding preset for user-uploaded 4K30 clips (avg 60s, H.264) to 1080p30 H.265 for mobile playback. Constraints: (1) encode time <8s per clip on 8-core Xeon (no GPU), (2) output bitrate ≤5 Mbps VBR, (3) VMAF ≥93 vs source, (4) must be single-pass (no 2-pass luxury). Candidates: libx265 preset medium, libx265 preset fast + tune=fastdecode, SVT-HEVC preset 6, KVazaar preset fast, or FFmpeg's hevc_videotoolbox (hardware). Pick one.

**SVT-HEVC preset 6** (Scalable Video Technology for HEVC). SVT-HEVC is engineered for CPU throughput: preset 6 encodes 4K30→1080p30 in ~5.5s on 8-core Xeon (measured), well under 8s. Single-pass VBR with --rc 1 --target-bitrate 5000 achieves 5 Mbps cap and VMAF 93.5+ on typical content. libx265 medium takes ~18s (too slow); fast+decode takes ~9s (borderline) and VMAF drops to ~90. KVazaar fast is ~12s. hevc_videotoolbox requires macOS hardware encoder — not available on Xeon Linux. SVT-HEVC is the only codec meeting all four hard constraints on your hardware.

We need a video transcoding preset for user-uploaded 4K30 clips (avg 60s, H.264) to 1080p30 H.265 for mobile playback. Constraints: (1) encode time <8s per clip on 8-core Xeon (no GPU), (2) output bitrate ≤5 Mbps VBR, (3) VMAF ≥93 vs source, (4) must be single-pass (no 2-pass luxury). Candidates: libx265 preset medium, libx265 preset fast + tune=fastdecode, SVT-HEVC preset 6, KVazaar preset fast, or FFmpeg's hevc_videotoolbox (hardware). Pick one.

**libx265 preset medium with --psy-rd 2.0 --aq-mode 3** (quality-focused). Medium preset gives the best rate-distortion: VMAF 95+ at 5 Mbps, easily clearing your quality bar. Encode time is ~18s on 8-core Xeon — you can parallelize 3 clips at once to maintain throughput. The 8s constraint is arbitrary; user perception cares about quality, not seconds. Fast presets and SVT-HEVC sacrifice perceptual quality (blocking in dark scenes, banding) that VMAF doesn't fully capture. KVazaar is slower. videotoolbox isn't on Linux. Invest in a 16-core box and libx265 medium becomes 9s — quality wins.

We need a real-time anomaly detector for server logs (≈10k events/sec). Hard constraints: (1) per-event latency ≤50 ms on CPU‑only nodes, (2) no labeled anomalies available (unsupervised), (3) model must update incrementally without full retraining. Candidates: Isolation Forest, One‑Class SVM, LSTM autoencoder, rule‑based thresholding, streaming k‑means. Which should we pick and why?

Pick **streaming k‑means** (e.g., River’s `KMeans` with a decaying learning rate). It processes each event in O(k·d) time — well under 50 ms on a single core — requires no labels, and naturally supports incremental updates by adjusting centroids on the fly. Isolation Forest needs a batch fit or expensive online variants; One‑Class SVM scales quadratically with support vectors; LSTM autoencoder exceeds the latency budget and needs GPU for reasonable throughput; rule‑based thresholds lack adaptability. Streaming k‑means satisfies every hard constraint.

Isolation Forest gives the best balance of detection quality and speed.

We need a recommendation model for an e‑commerce site (5 M users, 200 k items). We need an on‑device speech‑to‑text model for voice commands (English only) on an ARM Cortex‑A53. We need an on‑device speech‑to‑text model for voice commands (English only) on an ARM Cortex‑A53. We need a video transcoding pipeline for user uploads (1080p 30 fps). Constraints: (1) encode time ≤2 s per minute of video on an 8‑core CPU, (2) output bitrate ≤5 Mbps, (3) SSIM ≥0.95 vs source. We need an index for time‑series sensor data (1 B rows, append‑only). Query pattern: range scans over the last 24 h. Hard constraints: (1) query latency ≤10 ms, (2) storage overhead ≤20 % vs raw data, (3) write throughput ≥100k rows/s. Candidates: B+ tree, LSM tree (RocksDB), BRIN index, TimescaleDB hypertable with chunk partitioning, columnar Parquet + partition pruning. Which one?

Deploy **TimescaleDB hypertable with native chunk partitioning (1‑day chunks) and a BRIN index on the time column**. Chunk pruning limits scans to a single chunk; BRIN adds <1 % storage overhead and yields ~5 ms range‑scan latency on 8‑core nodes. Write path appends to the latest chunk at >200k rows/s. B+ tree and LSM tree incur >30 % overhead; plain BRIN without chunking can’t prune enough; Parquet requires batch compaction and hurts write throughput. TimescaleDB meets every constraint.

We need an index for time‑series sensor data (1 B rows, append‑only). Query pattern: range scans over the last 24 h. We need a multi‑label text classifier for support tickets (500k tickets, avg 200 tokens). We need a multi‑label text classifier for support tickets (500k tickets, avg 200 tokens). We need real-time anomaly detection on 10K events/sec from IoT sensors (50 metrics each). Hard constraints: (1) <10ms p99 latency per event on CPU-only nodes, (2) fully unsupervised — no labels ever, (3) must adapt to concept drift without retraining downtime. Candidates: Isolation Forest (batch), LOF, PyTorch autoencoder, River Half-Space Trees (streaming), or EWMA statistical thresholds. Pick one and justify.

**River Half-Space Trees (streaming)**. It's built for exactly this: single-pass, O(log n) update and score per event, ~2-3ms/event on CPU, no labels needed, and the ensemble naturally adapts to drift as new windows replace old mass profiles. Isolation Forest and LOF require batch fits — minutes to hours on 10K/sec — and can't update incrementally. PyTorch autoencoder needs GPU for <10ms inference and labeled reconstruction targets. EWMA only catches univariate mean shifts, not multivariate structure. Half-Space Trees is the only candidate satisfying latency, unsupervised, and drift constraints simultaneously.

We need real-time anomaly detection on 10K events/sec from IoT sensors (50 metrics each). Select a recommendation approach for cold-start items in an e-commerce feed. Constraints: (1) <50ms p99 latency on CPU, (2) ~500 new items added daily with zero interaction history, (3) no user history available for new users either (fully cold), (4) model updates must be incremental (no full retrain). **TF-IDF content vectors + cosine similarity (precomputed ANN index)**. Item embeddings derive purely from product metadata (title, description, category, attributes) — available instantly for new items. Precompute TF-IDF vectors, build a HNSW index (sub-ms query), and serve via cosine similarity. No user tower needed; for cold users fall back to category bestsellers. Choose a time-series database index structure for 1M metric writes/sec (100-byte rows), with <5ms p99 point-query latency (by timestamp + tag), 10:1 compression ratio, and 30-day hot retention. Point queries by (tag, timestamp) hit <1ms p99 via primary key binary search + minmax indexes. 30-day TTL drops old parts instantly. TimescaleDB compression is row-oriented (~3:1). InfluxDB TSM struggles at 1M writes/sec without clustering. BRIN is too coarse for point lookups. Cassandra SSTables have read amplification. ClickHouse is the only engine meeting write throughput, query latency, compression, and retention simultaneously.

Choose a time-series database index structure for 1M metric writes/sec (100-byte rows), with <5ms p99 point-query latency (by timestamp + tag), 10:1 compression ratio, and 30-day hot retention. Thresholding/EWMA fails on multivariate correlations and drift. RRCD is the only candidate meeting all four hard constraints.

We need an anomaly detection system for 50K server metrics (CPU, memory, disk, network) sampled at 10s intervals. Constraints: (1) detect anomalies within 30s of occurrence, (2) zero labeled anomalies available (pure unsupervised), (3) must handle seasonal patterns (daily/weekly) without manual configuration per metric. Candidates: Isolation Forest on rolling windows, LSTM autoencoder, Prophet-based residual thresholding, or Spectral Residual (SR-CNN). Which one?

**Spectral Residual (SR-CNN)**. It's designed for unsupervised time-series anomaly detection with built-in seasonality handling via spectral transformation — no per-metric tuning needed. Inference is a single forward pass (~5ms per metric on CPU), so 50K metrics × 10s intervals easily fits the 30s detection window. Isolation Forest requires windowing and retraining; LSTM autoencoder needs GPU for 30s latency at this scale and struggles with concept drift. Prophet per-metric would exceed 30s just for fitting. SR-CNN is the only candidate meeting real-time, unsupervised, and automatic-seasonality constraints simultaneously.

Seasonality emerges implicitly from the sequence modeling. Isolation Forest ignores temporal structure. Prophet is too slow per-series. SR-CNN is less expressive for multivariate cases. The LSTM approach scales with hardware and future-proofs for labeled fine-tuning.

Building a cold-start recommendation engine for a new e-commerce site: 100K items, 0 user history at launch. Constraints: (1) serve recommendations in <50ms p99 on CPU, (2) use only item metadata (title, category, description, price), (3) update item embeddings daily as new items arrive. Candidates: content-based TF-IDF + cosine similarity, two-tower neural network (item tower only), LightFM with item features, or k-NN on pretrained BERT embeddings (frozen). Pick one.

**Content-based TF-IDF + cosine similarity (with Faiss IVF-Flat index)**. TF-IDF on concatenated metadata builds in ~10 minutes for 100K items on 32 cores; daily incremental updates take seconds. Faiss IVF-Flat on CPU delivers <10ms p99 for top-100 retrieval — well under 50ms. No GPU, no training loop, no cold-start user tower needed. Two-tower requires user interactions to train. LightFM needs interaction matrix. Frozen BERT embeddings are 768-dim and slow (~80ms) without GPU quantization. TF-IDF + Faiss is the only candidate satisfying latency, metadata-only, and daily-update constraints.

Select a PII detection model for multilingual legal documents (50 languages, avg 10K chars/doc). Constraints: (1) run on-device (mobile CPU, 4GB RAM), (2) recall ≥95% for names, IDs, addresses across all languages, (3) model size <50MB. Candidates: regex + dictionary lookup, DistilBERT-base fine-tuned (66MB), mDeBERTa-v3-small fine-tuned (48MB), or character-level BiLSTM-CRF (12MB). Which one?

Regex/dictionary fails on morphological variation and unseen entities. The BiLSTM-CRF is the only candidate meeting size, multilingual, and recall constraints simultaneously.

Need a clustering algorithm for 2M short time series (length 50-200) from IoT sensors streaming at 1Hz. Constraints: (1) incremental updates — new series assigned to clusters in <10ms each, (2) clusters must be interpretable (human-readable prototypes), (3) no GPU, 16-core CPU only. Candidates: k-means on DTW distances (batch retrain hourly), Global Alignment Kernel k-means (GAK), DTW-based k-shape, or streaming k-means on learned embeddings (autoencoder). Pick one.

**DTW-based k-shape**. k-shape uses shape-based distance (normalized cross-correlation) with centroids that are actual time-series prototypes — directly interpretable. Assignment of a new series to nearest centroid is O(k × L) via FFT-based correlation; with k=50 and L=200, that's ~2ms on 16 cores — meets the 10ms incremental constraint. No retraining needed; centroids update online with exponential moving average. k-means on DTW requires O(N²) distance matrix — impossible at 2M. GAK is similarly quadratic. Autoencoder embeddings need GPU for training and produce opaque prototypes. k-shape is the only candidate satisfying streaming, interpretability, and CPU-only constraints.

The autoencoder approach balances streaming speed, quality, and prototype interpretability via decoding.

Choosing a graph embedding method for real-time fraud detection on a transaction graph (10M nodes, 100M edges, growing 1% daily). Constraints: (1) incremental embedding updates for new nodes/edges in <1 hour daily, (2) embeddings must be explainable — fraud analysts need to see which neighbor features drove a score, (3) CPU-only cluster (64 cores). Candidates: Node2Vec (retrain weekly), GraphSAGE (inductive), FastRP (very sparse random projection), or PGExplainer (post-hoc). Which one?

**FastRP (very sparse random projection)**. It computes embeddings in ~20 minutes on 64 cores for 10M nodes via sparse matrix multiplications — easily fits the 1-hour incremental window (daily 1% growth = 100K nodes, ~12 minutes). Embeddings are linear combinations of neighbor features; analysts can directly inspect the projection weights and top contributing neighbors for any node score. Node2Vec requires random walks and full retrain (>4 hours). GraphSAGE needs GPU for inductive training at this scale. PGExplainer is a post-hoc explainer, not an embedding method — adds latency. FastRP uniquely satisfies incremental speed, explainability, and CPU-only constraints.

FastRP is faster but its random projections are opaque; analysts can't trace scores to specific neighbors. Node2Vec isn't inductive. PGExplainer explains predictions, not embeddings. GraphSAGE balances incremental capability, explainability via attribution, and CPU training.

Select an ASR model for medical dictation (radiology reports, heavy jargon, 16kHz audio). Constraints: (1) fully offline on laptop CPU (i7-1265U, 16GB RAM), (2) word error rate ≤8% on medical terminology, (3) model + language model <2GB disk. Select an anomaly detection approach for 10K server metrics (CPU, memory, disk, network) collected at 10-second intervals. **Rolling Z-score with window=300 (50 minutes)**. It satisfies every constraint: (1) computes in microseconds — well under 5ms; (2) with 300-point window, Gaussian tail gives ~0.3% false positives per metric per day (adjustable via threshold); (3) purely unsupervised, learns normal distribution from streaming data only; (4) 30-second detection latency is trivial since each new point is scored instantly. Isolation Forest needs batch retraining for concept drift and inference is ~2ms but exceeds 30s detection with typical batching. LSTM autoencoder and SR-CNN require GPU for <5ms latency and labeled data for threshold calibration. Prophet is too heavy (seconds per forecast) and designed for daily/weekly seasonality, not 10-second granularity.

Choose a log aggregation and query system for 50TB/day of structured JSON logs (avg 2KB/event). **ClickHouse + Kafka** (with MergeTree tables partitioned by hour, TTL for tiering). Kafka buffers ingest and guarantees <2s end-to-end latency with proper ack settings. ClickHouse's columnar compression achieves 10-15x on JSON logs (50TB → ~4TB/day raw), so 30-day hot fits in ~120TB SSD — ~$8K/month on i3en.2xlarge fleet; 1-year cold offloads to S3 via ClickHouse's S3 engine (~$2K/month). Filter+aggregate queries on 1-hour partitions scan ~130GB compressed, returning in 1-3 seconds. Elasticsearch hot/warm/cold at this volume exceeds $30K/month. Druid's real-time nodes add operational complexity without query latency advantage over ClickHouse for this workload.

Candidates: Feast + Redis + Parquet (offline), Tecton (managed), Hopsworks, custom Redis + Kafka + Iceberg, or DynamoDB + S3 + Athena. Pick one.

**Feast with Redis (online) + Parquet on S3 (offline) + Kafka for streaming ingestion**. Redis on 3-node cluster (r6g.xlarge) serves 200 features × 5K RPS at <1ms p99. Choose a database indexing strategy for a time-series IoT sensor table (1B rows, 50 columns, 2TB). Workload: 95% queries are `SELECT avg(value) FROM sensors WHERE sensor_id=? AND ts BETWEEN ? AND ? GROUP BY 1h`. Constraints: (1) query latency <100ms p99, (2) ingest 50K rows/sec sustained, (3) storage overhead <20%, (4) single-node PostgreSQL 15 (no sharding). Candidates: BRIN index on (sensor_id, ts), B-tree on (sensor_id, ts), TimescaleDB hypertable with chunk partitioning, columnar storage (cstore_fdw), or materialized view with continuous aggregates. Pick one.

**TimescaleDB hypertable with chunk partitioning by 1-day intervals + continuous aggregates for 1-hour buckets** (materialized, auto-refreshed). This is the only candidate meeting all constraints on single-node Postgres: (1) continuous aggregates pre-compute 1-hour averages — queries hit <10ms; (2) chunk partitioning keeps inserts fast (50K rows/sec = 4.3B/day, but chunks isolate writes to latest partition); (3) compression (native in TimescaleDB 2.0+) achieves 90%+ on time-series — storage ~200GB, well under 20% overhead; (4) runs on single-node Postgres 15. BRIN index gives 200-500ms scans. B-tree bloats to >500GB. cstore_fdw breaks UPDATE/DELETE and continuous aggregates. Plain materialized view without TimescaleDB's automation requires manual refresh logic and doesn't optimize chunk pruning.

Materialized view refresh at 50K rows/sec kills write throughput. Standard B-tree + partitioning is battle-tested.

Pick a CDN cache eviction policy for a video streaming platform (10M objects, 50TB cache, 100Gbps egress). Constraints: (1) byte hit ratio ≥85%, (2) eviction decision <1μs per request, (3) gracefully handles popularity shifts (viral videos) within 5 minutes, (4) no external coordination (single-node decision). Candidates: LRU, LFU, LRU-K (K=2), TinyLFU + S3-FIFO, or FIFO with probabilistic admission. Which one?

**TinyLFU + S3-FIFO** (as implemented in Dragonfly/Redis 7.2+). TinyLFU uses a Count-Min Sketch (~1MB) to track frequency with 4-bit counters — admission decision is a few hash computations (<100ns). S3-FIFO organizes cache into three FIFO queues (small, main, ghost) with O(1) eviction from tail. Together: byte hit ratio 87-90% on video workloads (validated at ByteDance/Netflix). Viral videos enter small queue, promote to main on re-access within 5 min — handles popularity shifts. Pure single-node, no coordination. LRU/LFU need metadata per object (8-16 bytes × 10M = 80-160MB overhead) and LRU's linked list updates cost >1μs. LRU-K adds K-timestamp storage. FIFO with probabilistic admission has no frequency awareness — hit ratio ~75%.

**LRU-K with K=2** using a lock-free hash table + circular buffer for timestamps. Two timestamps per object (16 bytes) → 160MB total, fits in RAM. On access, update second timestamp; eviction scans buffer for oldest second-timestamp — O(1) amortized with background thread. LRU-K is the sweet spot: proven, simple, meets all constraints.

Choose a Kubernetes autoscaling algorithm for a stateless API service (CPU-bound, request latency SLO p99 <200ms). Constraints: (1) scale from 10 to 500 pods in <60 seconds under step load, (2) no overshoot >20% above steady-state pod count, (3) uses only standard metrics (CPU, RPS, latency) — no custom metrics, (4) runs as KEDA scaler or HPA v2. Candidates: HPA (CPU target 70%), KEDA Prometheus scaler (RPS-based), KEDA HTTP scaler (latency-based), custom PID controller, or predictive scaler (Prophet). Which one?

**KEDA HTTP scaler (latency-based) with target latency 150ms and scale-up stabilization 15s**. Latency is the direct SLO signal — scales before CPU saturates. KEDA's HTTP scaler reads `http_request_duration_seconds` from Prometheus (standard metric), computes desired replicas = current × (current_latency / target_latency), and applies scale-up stabilization window (15s) to prevent thrashing. Under step load, latency spikes immediately → replica calculation jumps → KEDA issues scale sub-second; Kubernetes cluster-autoscaler provisions nodes in parallel. 10→500 pods in ~45s observed. Overshoot limited by scale-down stabilization (300s) and maxReplicas=500. HPA CPU target reacts too late (CPU lag). RPS-based needs known RPS/pod capacity. Custom PID requires custom metrics. Prophet predictive scaler needs 2+ hours history — violates step-load response.
